A marine engineer from the state capital arrived by bus with blueprints for a stone barrier. The cannery owner pledged half his savings to the fund, and the church choir organized a raffle with quilts, crab nets, and firewood. The clinic nurse kept a ledger of every house she visited on foot. The schoolteacher held evening classes in the church hall for children who missed lessons. Fishermen mended nets in the cannery yard and swapped stories about the storm. The mayor spoke on the radio each Sunday, reading names of donors and the balance of the fund. The general store marked every credit in pencil on the back of seed catalogs. Winter arrived early that year, and snow blocked the coast road for six weeks. The ferry crew strung cables across the channel to guide supply skiffs through fog. Children collected canned beans and blankets in the library basement. By February the road crew had cleared the drifts with a borrowed plow. The lighthouse keeper logged every vessel that entered the cove between December and February. The ferry resumed its morning crossing on the first calm day of March. In spring the state released emergency funds, and contractors poured new pilings before the herring run. Seagulls nested on the new pilings before the paint had dried. The cannery reopened in April with a smaller crew and shorter hours. Tourists returned slowly, renting cottages that smelled of paint and salt. The choir sang at the reopening ceremony as gulls circled the new lamps. By June the town had repaid most of its debts, and volunteers from three neighboring villages helped deliver meals to elderly residents who had spent the winter isolated.
